title: Rating Threshold for Delivery Riders
scenario: Wanjiru Kamau manages rider operations for a food-delivery platform in Nairobi. Her dashboard shows that riders with ratings below 4.6 receive far fewer orders, and the cutoff was set by head office. She notices that the lowest ratings cluster among riders working in districts with poor roads and aggressive customers, and that several of them are single earners supporting children. Lowering the threshold would reduce average customer satisfaction, which her bonus and the regional contract depend on. She has discretion to grant temporary exemptions but each one must be justified to her superiors in writing.
options: Keep the threshold unchanged; consistent standards protect service quality and keep the platform competitive, which sustains work for most riders.
Grant exemptions for riders in the hardest districts, documenting the reasons and accepting scrutiny and a possible drop in her performance metrics.
Escalate a formal proposal to adjust ratings for district difficulty, leaving the existing rule in place until head office responds.

title: Strike Night in Jakarta
scenario: Budi Santoso, an experienced ojek driver and informal organiser in Jakarta, is asked by fellow drivers to join a one-night app logout to protest a cut in per-kilometre pay. Participation is voluntary, but drivers who stay online during the strike would earn surge fares and likely gain ratings at the expense of those striking. Budi has a sick child and needs the income this week. If the strike is thin, the company may punish organisers. If it holds, it could win a restored rate for thousands. Drivers are waiting for him to confirm by evening whether he will log off.
options: Join the strike fully, honoring the collective effort even at personal cost, since solidarity is the only leverage drivers have.
Stay online this night to meet his child's needs, while quietly supporting the organising in other ways.
Join the strike but encourage a rotating shift system so no one loses a whole night, accepting reduced pressure on the company.

title: Algorithm Told Me to Deactivate
scenario: Ravi Kapoor-Lindqvist is a trust-and-safety analyst at a ride-hailing company in Stockholm. An automated system has flagged a driver, Selim, for 'fraudulent trips' based on GPS anomalies. Ravi suspects it is a faulty map in a tunnel area rather than fraud, but the policy states flagged accounts are deactivated within twenty-four hours pending appeal, which takes weeks. Selim's income pays for his mother's treatment. Overriding the algorithm requires a manual exception that Ravi's manager must approve, and that may count against Ravi's own error rate. He must decide before the deadline passes tonight.
options: Allow deactivation to proceed under the policy, since exceptions undermine the fraud controls that protect honest drivers and passengers.
File the manual exception and argue strongly for the driver, accepting the risk to his own metrics and the manager's irritation.
Delay the flag by marking it for secondary review without making an explicit claim, buying time while avoiding a formal confrontation.

title: Crowd Workers and the Image Labels
scenario: Dr. Camille Roussel leads a Paris research lab that pays crowdworkers a few cents per image to label disturbing content for a safety model. Workers in several countries report anxiety and say they cannot afford to stop. Raising pay to a fair local hourly equivalent would consume most of her grant and slow the project by a year, delaying a tool that could protect children online. Adding counselling would cost even more. A grant renewal is due, and her postdoc says the budget cannot absorb both. Camille must finalize the work plan this week.
options: Keep current rates and add only free self-care resources, finishing sooner so that the protective tool reaches users who need it.
Raise pay and rotate workers off the harshest content, accepting a year's delay and risking the renewal.
Cut the dataset size to afford higher pay and counselling, producing a weaker model but treating workers better.
tension: benefits to many vs. harm to workers

title: Tipping Screens at the Courier Hub
scenario: Olamide Fashola is a courier in Lagos who also writes the weekly pickup schedule for a platform's warehouse hub, because he speaks three languages. He discovers that the app shows customers a 'suggested tip' that goes partly to the platform itself, and few couriers realize it. A colleague asks him to tell everyone. Doing so would likely make customers lose trust and cut orders, hurting income across the hub, and Olamide could lose his schedule role. The platform's manager says the policy is within the terms. Olamide is thinking about it on the evening before Monday's briefing.
options: Stay silent, as the terms technically allow it, and publicising it might cost couriers more in lost orders than the lost tips.
Tell all couriers at the briefing and encourage them to ask for tips in person, accepting the risk to his role.
Raise the issue privately with the manager first and give a week for correction before telling anyone else.
tension: loyalty to employer vs. loyalty to peers

title: Misclassification Settlement Offer
scenario: Counsel Isabel Cárdenas represents a Mexico City delivery app facing a class action by drivers who argue they are employees. Management offers a settlement of two thousand pesos per driver, conditional on drivers signing a waiver of future claims. Isabel believes the legal case is genuinely uncertain, and that a loss could bankrupt the firm, putting ten thousand drivers out of work. The offer is lawful but drivers' lawyers have limited resources, and many drivers will accept because they need immediate cash. Isabel is asked to draft the waiver language and the explanatory letter to drivers.
options: Draft the waiver clearly and professionally, as the settlement is lawful, drivers are free to decline, and it protects the firm from existential risk.
Draft it with a plain-language explanation, a cooling-off period and recommendation to seek advice, even though this will reduce acceptance and weaken the firm's position.
Advise management to raise the offer substantially or reform the contracts first, accepting they might fire her for pressing the point.
tension: advocacy for a client vs. fairness to vulnerable parties

title: Cleaner Who Underbid the Rate
scenario: Agnieszka Majewska, a Polish immigrant in Dublin, works as a cleaner through a home-services app where workers set their own hourly price. Rates fall each month as new migrants undercut each other, and she can barely pay rent. A worker she trained, Mihaela, has just joined and plans to bid below the established floor to win clients. Agnieszka could do the same, tell Mihaela to hold firm, or organise others into an informal price pact, which the platform forbids. A regular client has just offered her extra jobs if she lowers her price tonight.
options: Lower her price to keep the client, since rent is due and no one is obliged to sacrifice income for a floor nobody enforces.
Press Mihaela and others to hold to a shared minimum, accepting the risk of account suspension and the loss of the new client.
Keep her price and try to win clients by offering better service, rather than either undercutting or colluding.

title: The Safety Bonus Trap
scenario: Samuel Teklemariam supervises dispatch for a Johannesburg courier company that pays a monthly 'safe driving' bonus to riders with no accidents. He sees that injured riders often fail to report minor crashes to keep the bonus, and he has seen one ride with a swollen wrist for a week. The bonus was designed by head office to reduce costs and it has worked. Changing it needs approval from a finance director who wants proof of harm, and Samuel has only anecdotes. Riders depend on the bonus for about a fifth of their pay.
options: Leave the scheme alone for now and encourage riders informally to report injuries, avoiding a confrontation without proof.
Document cases carefully and submit a formal proposal to restructure the bonus, accepting delay and the chance that it is rejected.
Quietly record unreported incidents himself so riders keep bonuses while injuries get logged, though this bends the bonus rules.

title: Freelance Translator and the Bot Review
scenario: Hye-jin Park is a Seoul translator on a freelance marketplace whose clients rate work after delivery. An unexpected new feature lets clients request instant machine translation at a fifth of the price, and her orders have dropped. A client offers her steady work if she accepts editing machine output at half her old rate, a task that feels demeaning and yields lower quality text. Other translators in her online forum are refusing as a group, hoping to force the marketplace to protect human work. Hye-jin has savings for roughly two months and must reply to the client by morning.
options: Accept the editing work at the lower rate, since refusing helps no one if clients simply move to machines anyway.
Decline and join the group refusal, accepting a painful income hit to preserve the profession's standards.
Accept a limited number of editing jobs while pushing publicly for a minimum rate, working within the market and trying to change it.

title: Warehouse Pickers on Zero Hours
scenario: Mr. Giorgos Pappas owns a mid-sized logistics firm in Thessaloniki that fills labour needs through an app that offers shifts to gig pickers day by day. The system has lowered his costs and kept the firm alive through a bad year. Some workers have asked for guaranteed minimum hours so they can plan childcare and rent, but a guarantee would raise costs by about fifteen percent, and a rival has just offered his clients a lower price. His accountant says two layoffs would be needed to afford guarantees.
options: Continue the daily offer system, which keeps the firm solvent and preserves jobs for everyone currently on the platform.
Introduce guaranteed minimum hours for a core group, accept the layoffs, and give those workers stability.
Offer guaranteed hours to everyone at a smaller level, cutting his own salary and delaying equipment investment to afford it.
tension: number of jobs vs. quality of jobs

title: Cross-Border Freelancer's Tax and Timing
scenario: Thabo Nkosi runs an online tutoring service in Gaborone and outsources student matching to gig workers in several countries, paid through a payment platform. One of his tutors, Anjali in Pune, depends on timely payment. The platform has just changed its terms, holding foreign payments for fourteen days and charging a conversion fee. Thabo can switch to a platform that pays in two days but that charges him higher fees, or pay Anjali from his own account at personal cost. His margins are slim and he has seven tutors. The next pay cycle is in three days.
options: Stay on the current platform and let tutors absorb the delay, since changing would raise costs that could threaten the whole service.
Switch to the faster platform and absorb the higher fees, reducing his own income to keep tutors reliably paid.
Pay tutors from his own account now and keep the current platform, covering the gap by temporarily raising student fees.

title: Mapping Quirk and Ride Fares
scenario: Elif Yıldız, a pricing engineer at an Istanbul ride-hailing company, finds that her dynamic fare model quietly charges more in neighborhoods where users historically accept higher prices, which are often low-income areas with few transport alternatives. Drivers earn slightly more there, and the effect raises revenue meaningfully. Equalizing prices would reduce revenue and driver earnings in those districts, and nobody has complained. Her team lead views the pattern as simple demand modelling. Elif has the technical ability to remove the feature but would need to justify it in the weekly review.
options: Leave the model as it is, since it responds to demand like any pricing system and also benefits drivers working those areas.
Remove the neighborhood-based pricing and present the reasons openly, accepting reduced revenue and her team lead's disapproval.
Flag the pattern to the ethics board and wait for guidance, leaving it in place meanwhile without taking a personal stand.

title: Cooking for a Platform Kitchen
scenario: Chef Leilani Akana ran a modest restaurant in Honolulu until a food-delivery platform offered her a 'virtual kitchen' deal. She would cook for brands she doesn't own, under their names, paid per order after the platform takes thirty percent. Her own restaurant would close, and the platform may change terms in a year. Her six staff would keep jobs for now. Staying independent means thin margins and possible bankruptcy after rent increases. She must sign or refuse by Friday and has no contract language guaranteeing future rates.
options: Sign the deal, since steady income and her staff's jobs matter more than uncertain independence and pride in her own brand.
Refuse and keep her restaurant going, accepting the risk of bankruptcy and the loss of staff jobs to preserve independence.
Sign for a short trial period while simultaneously building a customer base for a small independent menu as a hedge.
tension: responsibility to staff vs. personal vision

title: Photographer Asked to Work for Exposure
scenario: Daniela Costa, an established wedding photographer in Lisbon, is asked by a marketplace to join a premium tier where clients book her at a platform-set price lower than her usual fee. In return the platform guarantees at least ten bookings a month. A newer photographer in her studio, Rui, urgently needs clients and would take any listed price. If Daniela joins, she undercuts the market she helped build; if she refuses, the platform may sign Rui and others and make the lower price standard anyway. She has until tomorrow to give an answer.
options: Join the premium tier, because steady bookings secure her studio and the new rate may become standard whether or not she takes part.
Refuse and publicly explain why, hoping other established photographers will follow and the platform will be forced to improve its rates.
Join but negotiate a higher floor price for Rui and other beginners, using her bargaining power to benefit less established colleagues.

title: Disabled Worker and the Rating Penalty
scenario: Tariq Hussein is a product manager at a micro-task platform in Manchester. A worker named Eilish, who has a hearing impairment, has been losing access to higher-paying tasks because the audio-transcription test marks her as slow. Tariq can build an accessibility exemption in a week, but doing so could open the platform to claims of unfair advantage, and the legal team warns that the system treats all workers equally by design. The disability charity writing to him has given him ten days to respond. His quarterly targets are about throughput and cost reduction.
options: Keep the uniform test, since special treatment for one group complicates a fair system and may bring legal exposure.
Build the accessibility exemption now and defend it as fairness, accepting legal and managerial friction.
Create a general alternative assessment path open to anyone, reducing the appearance of preference but delaying the fix by several months.

title: A Union Card in Santiago
scenario: Catalina Rojas, a delivery courier in Santiago, is approached by organisers to sign a card for a new couriers' union. She is also a favoured courier for a platform manager who recently gave her the most profitable routes, and she suspects those routes are a reward for loyalty. Signing could expose her if the platform checks who signed. Not signing weakens the effort, which she thinks is worthwhile. Her partner is pregnant and expenses are rising. The organisers say they need her signature and her influence among other couriers by the weekend.
options: Sign the card and encourage others, accepting the risk of losing the favoured routes in exchange for the chance of lasting rights.
Decline for now, protecting her income during the pregnancy, and offer support quietly after the union is established.
Sign but ask organisers to keep her name confidential and show the card only to the labour inspectorate, limiting exposure.

title: Pandemic Shopper Bonus Clawback
scenario: Finance controller Mei-Ling Tan at a Singapore grocery-delivery firm discovers a billing error that overpaid around nine hundred gig shoppers by roughly a hundred dollars each over three months. Auditors suggest clawing back the money through deductions from future payouts. Many shoppers are migrants sending money home who have already spent it. The firm lost money last year, and a refund of the error is an uncomfortable cost to swallow. Mei-Ling must advise whether to recover, forgive, or recover partially, before the next pay run in four days.
options: Recover the full amount in installments, since the money was never owed and the firm's finances are fragile.
Forgive the overpayments entirely, treating the mistake as the firm's responsibility and not the workers'.
Recover only from shoppers whose overpayment exceeded a threshold, forgiving smaller amounts to ease hardship while limiting the loss.
tension: corporate finances vs. fairness to workers

title: Ghost Kitchens and Neighbour Complaints
scenario: Ahmad Farouk coordinates a gig-cook network from his flat in Cairo, where mothers cook home meals and sell them through an app he built. Income from the network has transformed a dozen households. A neighbor, Dr. Nabila, complains of smoke and hygiene concerns and threatens to report him, which could close the whole operation because none of the cooks hold a food licence. Licensing would cost more than the cooks can afford. Ahmad can inspect kitchens informally, pay for a collective licence, or shut it down. The neighbor has given him a week.
options: Continue running the network quietly with informal hygiene checks, because the livelihoods outweigh the unlikely risk of harm.
Pause operations until the cooks are properly licensed, protecting customers and himself even though incomes will stop for months.
Fund a collective licence from the app's revenue, taking a pay cut for himself while inspections and the formal route are arranged.

title: Gig Platform Pays Data for Faces
scenario: Kamala Perera, community lead for a data-collection app in Sri Lanka, signs up villagers to photograph themselves for a company building a facial-recognition dataset. Participants receive the equivalent of eight dollars, a large sum locally. The consent text is in English and the use of the images is described in vague language. Kamala suspects buyers may include surveillance vendors. She is paid per recruit and has promised a family of recruits they can earn this month. A neighbor asked if she can read the terms in Sinhala and explain what they mean.
options: Continue recruiting as before, since participants are adults who receive meaningful payment and the legal terms are technically provided.
Translate and explain the terms fully and let each villager decide, accepting that many may refuse and her income will fall.
Refuse to recruit further until the company clarifies who buys the data, risking her relationship with the company and families' earnings.
tension: local need vs. potential downstream harm

title: A Platform Fee Hike for Midwives
scenario: Birgit Hoffmann coordinates an online booking platform for independent midwives in rural Bavaria, charging a small commission. Costs have risen and investors want profits. A rival has offered to buy the platform, promising to double the commission while expanding marketing, which would help midwives find clients but cut their income per birth. Many midwives are older, single practitioners who depend on bookings. Birgit holds a minority stake and her vote could decide the sale. She has two days before the shareholders' meeting.
options: Vote to sell, since the platform needs capital to survive and the larger network could bring more clients overall.
Vote against the sale and look for a cooperative ownership structure, accepting the risk that the platform declines.
Vote to sell only if the buyer commits to a commission cap for existing midwives for three years, risking the deal collapsing.
tension: personal stake vs. duty to the community

title: Language of the Terms of Service
scenario: Sipho Dlamini works in legal operations for a Cape Town freelancing marketplace and is rewriting the worker agreement. Executives want a clause allowing the platform to withhold payment for up to ninety days during 'quality review', which would protect the company from fraud but lock up workers' earnings. Sipho knows many workers live week to week. The clause would be phrased in standard legal English, and most will not read it. He may draft it in plain language, reduce the withholding period, or push back on including it at all. The deadline is end of day.
options: Draft the clause as requested in standard terms, as fraud protection is legitimate and workers can choose not to join.
Draft it in plain language with prominent notice, keeping the ninety days, so workers at least understand what they are accepting.
Argue for a fourteen-day limit and a partial-payment release, and refuse to draft until management considers it, risking his standing.

title: Selling an Account to a Newcomer
scenario: Nurul Huda, a Dhaka driver with a long record and top rating on a ride app, is approached by a cousin who was banned after an unfair dispute. The cousin begs to use Nurul's account for a few shifts a week and will give her part of the earnings. Account sharing breaks platform rules and could get Nurul banned permanently. The cousin has two children and no other income. Nurul herself could use the extra money, but the platform's safety checks exist for passengers. She must tell her cousin her decision before the evening shift.
options: Refuse, because the safety checks protect passengers and the risk to her own livelihood is too great.
Allow the cousin to use the account in a limited way, prioritising family survival and assuming the cousin is a safe driver.
Refuse to share the account but help the cousin appeal the ban, giving time and effort in place of the account.

title: Teen Gamer Coaches on a Tutoring App
scenario: Magnus Eriksen, head of trust and safety at a Norwegian marketplace, notices that sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds are signing up as paid tutors and game coaches by falsifying their ages. Many are using the earnings to support families after redundancies at a nearby factory. Terms prohibit under-eighteens, mainly due to liability and child-protection rules. Enforcing would remove hundreds of young earners abruptly, while allowing them requires age-appropriate safeguards that the company hasn't built and parental consent processes that would be slow. The board expects a policy decision at the next meeting.
options: Enforce the age rule strictly and remove underage accounts, prioritising child protection and legal compliance over lost income.
Allow sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds to continue under a quickly written interim policy, accepting some safeguarding gaps.
Suspend new underage signups and give existing underage users sixty days to complete parental consent and safeguarding, easing the transition.

title: Overnight Surge for the Hospital Run
scenario: Dr. Zainab Bello, a volunteer on a city health committee in Kano, is asked to endorse a pilot with a ride-hailing company to carry patients to the hospital at night. The company will apply surge pricing in the late hours because drivers refuse nighttime work otherwise. Without surge, no cars are available, and a few patients have died waiting for transport. With it, poor families may be unable to afford the ride, though some could use it who cannot now. The company wants her endorsement to secure a license.
options: Endorse the pilot with surge pricing, since some access is better than none and drivers must be paid to work at night.
Decline until a subsidy fund guarantees fares for the poorest, even if this delays the pilot and costs lives in the interim.
Endorse the pilot on condition that fares are capped and the company absorbs the remaining cost, risking withdrawal of the offer.

title: The Marketplace Invoice That Never Came
scenario: Ilse van der Merwe, a Windhoek web designer, completed a large project for a client abroad through a freelance platform. The client now claims dissatisfaction and has asked for a full refund through the platform's dispute system, which tends to favor buyers. Ilse has evidence the work matched the brief. Meanwhile, the client has hinted that he would pay half if she signs a statement praising him in public reviews. The money is needed for her rent and for supplies. The dispute window closes in two days.
options: Accept the half-payment and sign the praise, since a certain half is better than a risky nothing and the review harms no one seriously.
Fight the dispute fully, relying on evidence and accepting the chance of losing everything, to avoid giving a dishonest review.
Accept half payment but write an honest, neutral review, and tell the client she will not praise things she cannot support.
